title: Legal Issues & Land Title
overview: How New York ownership changes hands: deeds, delivery, recording, title searches and insurance, legal descriptions, adverse possession, inheritance, escheat, and eminent domain. The exam hits three ideas hardest: **title passes on delivery**, not recording; a later buyer wins only as a good-faith purchaser for value who **records first**; and deed forms differ in what they promise.

mustKnow: **Title** is ownership; a **deed** is the writing that transfers it. The grantor conveys and the grantee receives.

A valid deed needs a writing, a competent grantor, a living, identifiable grantee, words of conveyance, a consideration recital, a legal description, the grantor's signature, and **delivery and acceptance**.
Only the **grantor** must sign. Grantees need no capacity, but a deed to a grantee who **died before delivery** is void.
A **minor's** deed (under 18) is **voidable**, not void, and recording doesn't cure it.
Deeds need no witnesses. **Acknowledgment** is needed only to **record**, not for validity.
**Title passes on delivery and acceptance**, not at signing and not at recording.
**Delivery** means giving up control with **present intent**. A deed kept in the grantor's safe, or held by her own attorney until she decides, isn't delivered.
Acceptance is presumed for a beneficial deed, but an **express refusal** defeats it. Destroying or returning a delivered deed **doesn't reconvey** the land.
**Recording** gives constructive notice and priority. It can't pass title, cure non-delivery, or validate a **forged deed**.
New York is a **race-notice** state: a later buyer wins only as a good-faith purchaser for value who **records first** (RPL §291).
Donees and heirs can't use the recording act to defeat an earlier unrecorded deed. **Mortgagees for value** can.
Someone other than the seller **in possession** gives **inquiry notice**.
Record with the **county clerk** where the land lies. Most of NYC records with the City Register through **ACRIS**.
Deed strength: **full covenant and warranty > bargain and sale with covenant > bargain and sale without covenants > quitclaim**.
The five covenants: **seisin, quiet enjoyment, against encumbrances, further assurances, warranty**. Seisin and against encumbrances are **present** covenants.
The **bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts** is the usual NY residential deed; it covers only the **seller's own** acts.
A **quitclaim** passes whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties. It's the standard way to clear a **cloud on title**.
**Referee's deed** = foreclosure or partition sale.
**Executor's deed** = estate with a will; **administrator's deed** = estate without one.
**Granting clause** = words of conveyance; **habendum** ('to have and to hold') = the estate granted.
An **exception** keeps land out of the deed; a **reservation** keeps a new right such as an easement. 'Subject to' lists encumbrances the buyer accepts.
NY deeds usually recite nominal consideration. The real price goes on the **TP-584**, which both parties sign, and the **RP-5217**.
The RP-5217 gives sale data to assessors and ORPTS, the state Office of Real Property Tax Services.
NYS transfer tax: **$2 per $500 or fraction**, units rounded up, paid by the **seller**.
**Chain of title** = owner-to-owner links; abstract = summary of every recorded document; **marketable title** = free of reasonable doubt.
An **owner's policy** covers the buyer and heirs while they own; a **lender's policy** covers only the lender, up to the loan balance. NY buyers customarily pay for both, once, at closing.
Title insurance covers **hidden defects existing on the policy date**. Survey matters and **parties in possession** are standard exceptions.
**Metes and bounds** starts and ends at the point of beginning, and **monuments beat distances**.
Bearings run from N or S toward E or W. Reversing a line **flips both letters** (N 60° E becomes S 60° W).
NY uses metes and bounds, filed maps, and tax maps, not the **rectangular survey**. **1 acre = 43,560 sq ft**.
**Adverse possession** takes **10 years** of hostile, actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous possession under claim of right. Paying taxes isn't required, and tacking is allowed.
Since 2008, **claim of right** means a reasonable basis to believe you own the land.
Since 2008, de minimis fences, hedges, and sheds, plus mowing, are **permissive**.
A **quiet title** judgment makes an adverse possessor's title marketable.
Intestate with spouse and issue: the spouse gets **$50,000 + half the rest**. With no issue, the spouse takes **everything**.
The **elective share** is the greater of **$50,000 or ⅓**.
A will needs a testator 18+, a signature **at the end**, and **two witnesses** signing within 30 days. Holographic wills count only for wartime military and mariners at sea.
**Devise** = real property by will; **bequest** = personal property; probate = the Surrogate's Court proving the will.
**Escheat** happens only if **no distributee** survives.
**Eminent domain** requires **just compensation**, plus severance damages after a partial taking.

traps.trap: Title passes when the deed is recorded.
traps.truth: Title passes on delivery and acceptance; recording only gives notice and priority.

traps.trap: A deed that isn't notarized or witnessed is invalid.
traps.truth: The deed is valid between the parties; NY requires no witnesses for validity. Without an acknowledgment, or proof by a subscribing witness, it can't be recorded.
Only a good-faith purchaser for value who records first wins. A donee, or a buyer with notice, loses even after recording first.

traps.trap: Recording a forged deed protects the innocent buyer who records.
traps.truth: A forged deed is void, and recording can't fix that. Title insurance is the protection.

traps.trap: A quitclaim conveys nothing, or only a defective title.
traps.truth: A quitclaim conveys whatever the grantor owns, possibly full title. It just carries no warranties.

traps.trap: A bargain and sale deed without covenants is the same as a quitclaim.
traps.truth: The quitclaim is weaker. The bargain and sale deed's granting words imply the grantor has title; a quitclaim implies nothing.

traps.trap: A bargain and sale deed with covenant protects against an earlier owner's liens.
traps.truth: Its covenant covers only what the grantor did or allowed. Only the full covenant deed reaches older defects.

traps.trap: The lender's title policy protects the buyer too.
traps.truth: It protects only the lender. The buyer needs an owner's policy, and the seller's old policy doesn't pass to the buyer.

traps.trap: Title insurance covers title problems that arise after closing.
traps.truth: A standard policy covers only defects that existed on the policy date, subject to its exceptions. Only enhanced homeowner's policies add a few later risks, such as post-closing forgery.

traps.trap: Ten years of using a neighbor's strip automatically gives title.
traps.truth: Every element must be proven, including claim of right. Mowing and de minimis fences, hedges, and sheds are permissive. Paying the taxes is neither required nor enough.

traps.trap: Dying without a will sends property to the state.
traps.truth: Escheat happens only if no distributee survives; even a first cousin inherits ahead of the state.

traps.trap: A spouse with no children shares the estate with the decedent's parents.
traps.truth: With no issue, the spouse takes everything; parents inherit only if there's no spouse and no issue.

traps.trap: A signed, handwritten will is valid, especially if notarized.
traps.truth: Everyone except wartime military and mariners at sea needs two witnesses, and notarizing can't replace them. Only those groups can use unwitnessed handwritten wills.

traps.trap: The court appoints an executor when there's no will.
traps.truth: With no will, the court appoints an administrator. An executor is named in a will.
One acre is 43,560 sq ft (4,840 sq yd).

sections.heading: What makes a deed valid
sections.intro: A **deed** is the written instrument that transfers **title** (ownership) of real property. The sale contract promises a conveyance; the deed delivered at closing makes it.
points: The **grantor** ('party of the first part' on NY forms) conveys. The **grantee** ('party of the second part') receives.
A **conveyance** is the transfer or the document that makes it. **Alienation** is any transfer of ownership.
A conveyance must be **in writing and subscribed by the grantor**, or by an agent authorized in writing such as an attorney-in-fact (General Obligations Law §5-703).
A **minor's** deed is **voidable**: it stands unless the minor disaffirms it. A grantor who lacked mental capacity can have the deed set aside. Recording cures neither.
The **grantee** must be identifiable and **alive at delivery**; an entity grantee must already exist. A deed to someone already dead is void. Minors can be grantees.

Unstated shares are presumed equal. Co-grantees take as **tenants in common** unless the deed expressly creates a joint tenancy. Spouses take as **tenants by the entirety** unless the deed says otherwise (EPTL §6-2.2).
A grantor conveys only what she owns. If one of two tenants in common signs a deed for 'the property,' the buyer gets only her undivided share.
Validity needs no **witnesses** and no grantee's signature. A grantee signs only to take on a duty, such as assuming the seller's mortgage (GOL §5-705).
**Acknowledgment** matters only for recording.

sections.heading: Deed clauses and their wording
sections.intro: Questions often quote deed language and ask which clause it is.
points: NY deeds usually recite **nominal consideration**. The real price is reported on the TP-584 and RP-5217.
A **gift deed** is valid. But a donee isn't a purchaser for value, so the recording act protects a donee less.
**Exception:** that piece never passes, and the grantor keeps owning it. **Reservation:** the land passes, but the grantor keeps a new right in it, usually an easement.
'**Subject to**' language lets the buyer take title burdened by the listed encumbrances without a covenant claim against the grantor. It neither creates nor ends them.
Discriminatory restrictions in old deeds are unenforceable.
A **correction deed** from the same grantor to the same grantee fixes clerical errors, such as a misspelled name or a transposed lot number, without a new sale.

sections.heading: Covenants in a full covenant and warranty deed
sections.intro: A **covenant** is a promise in the deed. New York's statutory full covenant and warranty deed has five (RPL §§253, 258). Books that count six split 'right to convey' out of seisin.
points: **Present** covenants (seisin, against encumbrances) are breached at delivery or never.
**Future** covenants (quiet enjoyment, further assurances, warranty) are breached later, when a superior claim surfaces.
Only this deed warrants against defects from **any period**, including those created before the grantor owned the land.
The **covenant against grantor's acts** says the grantor 'has not done or suffered anything' to encumber the land. It isn't one of the five.
It's the only title covenant in the bargain and sale deed with covenant and in the statutory executor's deed.

head: Covenant
The grantor promises
Type
rows: I own this estate and may convey it
No liens or encumbrances except those listed
No one with better title will disturb you
I'll sign anything else needed to perfect your title
I'll forever defend your title against all lawful claims

sections.heading: Forms of deeds, ranked by protection
sections.intro: New York's statutory deed forms are optional (RPL §258). The sale contract decides which one the seller must deliver.
points: The **bargain and sale deed with covenant** is the usual New York residential deed. Other states call the closest equivalent a special warranty deed.
A judgment lien against an earlier owner falls outside its covenant. Title insurance handles that.
A **bargain and sale deed without covenants** says 'grant and release,' which implies the grantor has title.
A **quitclaim** ('remise, release and quitclaim') implies nothing, so it's the weakest deed. It still passes full title if the grantor has it.
A quitclaim is the standard cure for a **cloud on title**, such as a possible claim by an heir or ex-spouse.
**Court and fiduciary deeds** carry no full warranties.
NY residential foreclosures are court cases, so the winning bidder gets a **referee's deed**. A court-ordered partition sale between co-owners ends the same way.

What the grantor promises
Typical use
rows: All five covenants, against claims from any era
Implied title; grantor did nothing to encumber it

sections.heading: Delivery and acceptance
sections.intro: Title passes at delivery and acceptance, so these questions turn on whether the grantor truly let go.
points: **Delivery** means the grantor gives up control with the **intent that title pass now**. The deed goes to the grantee or the grantee's agent, such as an attorney or title company.
**Not delivered:** a deed kept in the grantor's own safe-deposit box, held by the grantor's own attorney until she decides, or found after death.
Delivery must happen **during the grantor's life**.
An **escrow** agent holding the deed under **irrevocable instructions** is different. The grantor can't recall it, so delivery can be valid.
**Acceptance** is presumed when the deed benefits the grantee. An **express refusal**, such as mailing back a deed to a contaminated lot, means title never passed.
After delivery, returning or tearing up the deed **doesn't reconvey** the land.
Recording raises a presumption of delivery but **can't cure non-delivery**.
Sequence: grantor signs → acknowledges → delivers, grantee accepts (title passes) → grantee records.

sections.heading: Acknowledgment and recording (race-notice)
sections.intro: Acknowledgment makes a deed recordable. Recording gives the world notice and gives the grantee priority.
points: **Acknowledgment:** the grantor declares before a notary or other authorized officer that the signature is genuine and voluntary (RPL §298). It makes the deed **recordable**.
Acknowledgment doesn't pass title or give notice.
An unacknowledged deed is **valid between the parties** but **can't be recorded** unless proved by a subscribing witness. So it gives no constructive notice.
Record with the **county clerk** where the land lies. An Albany house goes to the Albany County Clerk, not the assessor.

In NYC, Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens record with the **City Register** through ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. Staten Island records with the **Richmond County Clerk**.
**Race-notice:** an unrecorded deed is void against a later buyer who takes in good faith (no notice), for value, and **records first** (RPL §291).
A pure race statute would ignore notice. A pure notice statute would ignore who records first.
Protected: buyers and **mortgagees** who give value. A mortgage counts as a conveyance (RPL §290).
Not protected: **donees**, heirs, and anyone with notice.
Recording can't validate a **forged** or void deed, cure non-delivery or incapacity, or guarantee title.
A recorded **notice of pendency (lis pendens)** warns of a lawsuit affecting title but decides nothing.
'First recorded wins' isn't absolute: real estate tax liens take priority anyway.

Meaning
Example

A properly recorded deed or mortgage

example.title: Worked example: who wins under race-notice?
steps: Owner sells a lot to Ana, who doesn't record, then sells the same lot to Ben.
Step 1, good faith: if Ben knew of Ana's deed, or Ana was visibly living there, Ben loses regardless of recording.
Step 2, value: if Ben received the lot as a gift, he can't defeat Ana.
Step 3, the race: Ben paid value without notice. If he records before Ana, he wins, and Ana sues Owner.
Step 4: if Ana records first, Ana wins.
Answer: the later buyer wins only with all three: good faith, value, and recording first.

sections.heading: Transfer forms and the transfer tax
sections.intro: Tax and reporting forms are filed along with the deed.
points: **NYS transfer tax:** $2 per $500 of consideration or fraction thereof, paid by the **seller**. The buyer is liable if the seller doesn't pay or is exempt (Tax Law §§1402, 1404).
The TP-584 also reports the **1% mansion tax**. The **buyer** pays it on residential sales of $1 million or more, on the full price.
In NYC, the seller also pays the city transfer tax. Residential rates: 1% at $500,000 or less; 1.425% of the full price above that.
Big sales owe extra state tax. The base rate rises to $3.25 per $500 at residential $3 million+ (other property $2 million+).
The buyer's mansion tax climbs in steps from 1.25% at residential $2 million+ to 3.9% at $25 million+.
The **RP-5217** is required to record a deed (RPL §333(1-e)). Mortgage recording tax is a separate tax on the loan.
**ACRIS** is NYC's land-records system. eAccessNY is the DOS licensing portal, unrelated to deeds.

steps: A house outside NYC sells for $512,300.
Step 2: Any fraction counts as a full unit: 1,025 units.
Answer: $2,050, paid by the seller. Distractors: $2,049.20 (no round-up), $2,048 (rounded down), $5,123 (1%).

sections.heading: Title search, chain of title, and clouds
sections.intro: A **title search** of the public records confirms the seller owns what's being sold and finds liens and encumbrances.
points: The **title report** (commitment) lists what must be paid off or cleared before closing and what the insurer won't cover.
**Chain of title** is the sequence of ownership transfers. An **abstract of title** is a condensed summary of every recorded instrument: deeds, mortgages, liens, easements.
A missing link in the chain is a **gap**. Any claim casting doubt on ownership is a **cloud**.
**Marketable title** is free from reasonable doubt, acceptable to a prudent, informed buyer.
Marketability is measured against the contract. An easement the buyer agreed to take subject to doesn't make title unmarketable.

Records can't reveal a forged deed, or rights created without any document: a **prescriptive easement**, adverse possession, someone in possession. Inspection, a survey, and title insurance fill those gaps.

sections.heading: Title insurance
sections.intro: **Title insurance** covers losses from title defects that existed on the policy date, except listed exceptions. The premium is paid once, at closing. The Department of Financial Services regulates it (Insurance Law Article 64).
points: **Covered:** forgery, a past grantor's incapacity, missing heirs, indexing errors. The insurer **defends the title** and pays covered losses up to the policy amount.
**Not covered** by a standard policy: defects arising **after** the policy date (a neighbor's shed built later), listed exceptions, and physical damage.
An enhanced homeowner's policy adds a few post-closing risks, such as later forgery or a neighbor's later-built structure other than a fence or wall.
Unless a question says the policy is enhanced, apply the standard rule.
**Standard exceptions:** survey matters such as encroachments, and **parties in possession**.
A **survey reading** compares a survey with the deed description and swaps the general survey exception for specific ones. So 'never covers encroachments' is too broad.
With a $500,000 price and a $400,000 loan, the lender's policy is $400,000 and protects only the bank.
An owner's policy never passes to the next buyer.

head: Feature
Owner's policy
Lender's policy
rows: While insured or heirs hold an interest
Shrinks with the loan; ends at payoff

sections.heading: Legal descriptions, surveys, and acreage
sections.intro: A **legal description** lets a surveyor find the exact parcel. New York deeds use metes and bounds, filed-map references, or both, often alongside tax map numbers.
points: **Metes** are distances and **bounds** are directions.
A description starts at the **point of beginning (POB)** and must return to it.
**Bearings** start at north or south and turn up to 90° toward east or west. S 30° W means face south, then turn 30° west.
Reverse a line by **flipping both letters**: N 60° E becomes S 60° W.
**Monuments** (an iron pipe, a stone wall, a stream) **control over distances**. 'North 200 feet to an iron pipe' with the pipe at 204 feet means the pipe wins.
A **filed plat** reference: 'Lot 14 on the map of Maple Ridge Estates, filed as Map No. 3127.' In NYC, 'Block 1450, Lot 22' comes from the **tax map**.
A **survey** by a licensed land surveyor locates boundaries, improvements, encroachments, and easements.
A **datum** is the base level for elevations, such as mean sea level. A **benchmark** is a marker of known elevation.
Area: rectangle = length × width; triangle = ½ × base × height. **1 acre = 43,560 sq ft**; 1 square mile = 640 acres.

head: Method
How it works
Used in NY?
rows: Courses and distances from a POB and back
Lot on a subdivision map filed with the county clerk
Section, block, and lot (borough, block, and lot in NYC)
Yes, usually with a full description

example.title: Worked example: acreage of an irregular lot
steps: A parcel is a 400 ft × 217.8 ft rectangle plus a right triangle with legs of 200 ft and 217.8 ft. Land sells for $36,000 per acre.
Step 1: Rectangle = 400 × 217.8 = 87,120 sq ft.
Step 2: Triangle = ½ × 200 × 217.8 = 21,780 sq ft.
Step 3: Total = 108,900 sq ft ÷ 43,560 = 2.5 acres.
Answer: 2.5 acres, worth $90,000.

sections.heading: Adverse possession in New York
sections.intro: **Adverse possession** gives title to someone who meets every element for **10 years** (CPLR 212(a); RPAPL Article 5). It's involuntary alienation, tightened in 2008.
points: **2008 amendments** (effective July 7, 2008): someone who knowingly takes an identifiable neighbor's land has no claim of right. Minor encroachments and mowing are permissive.
If the 10 years ended before July 7, 2008, title already vested under the old law.
Paying **taxes** isn't required.
**Tacking:** possessors in privity, such as seller and buyer, add their time together (6 + 5 = 11 years).
Title **vests automatically** at 10 years. A **quiet title** judgment makes it recordable and marketable (RPAPL Article 15).
Government land held for a **public use** (streets, parks) can't be adversely possessed.
A **prescriptive easement** is a 10-year **use** right, such as driving across a side yard. It isn't ownership, and it won't show up in a records search.

head: Element
Meaning
NY detail
rows: Reasonable basis to believe you own it
Excused if the owner can't be found in county records or by reasonable means (RPAPL §501(3))
De minimis fences, hedges, shrubs, sheds, and mowing are permissive (RPAPL §543)
Using the land as an owner would
If not under a written instrument: acts open enough to notify a diligent owner, or a substantial enclosure (RPAPL §522)

sections.heading: Transfers at death: wills, intestacy, and escheat
sections.intro: Property passes under a will (**testate**) or under the intestacy statute (**intestate**). In New York, the Surrogate's Court supervises both.
points: **Testate:** probate proves the will, and the court issues letters testamentary to the **executor** named in it. The executor sells with an executor's deed.
**Intestate:** the court appoints an **administrator** and issues letters of administration. The administrator signs an administrator's deed.
A **testator** makes a will, and a **codicil** amends it. Testatrix, executrix, and administratrix are older female forms.
A **devise** is real property by will, to a devisee. A **bequest** or legacy is personal property.
Heirs under intestacy are **distributees**, and they take **title by descent**.
**Executing a will:** the testator must be 18+ and of sound mind. The will must be in writing, **signed at the end**, and declared to be the will.
A will needs **two attesting witnesses** who sign within one 30-day period. No notary is needed (EPTL §§3-1.1, 3-2.1).

**Holographic** (handwritten, unwitnessed) and oral wills are valid only for armed forces members in war or armed conflict, those accompanying them, and mariners at sea. They also expire (EPTL §3-2.2).
**Elective share:** a disinherited spouse can elect the greater of **$50,000 or ⅓ of the net estate** (EPTL §5-1.1-A). A $600,000 estate left to charity lets the wife elect $200,000.
**Escheat** happens only if **no distributee** survives; a first cousin still inherits.
Books split on whether descent is voluntary or involuntary, but escheat is always involuntary.

head: Survivors (intestate)
Who takes (EPTL §4-1.1)
rows: Spouse: $50,000 + ½ of the rest; issue: the balance
Siblings or their descendants (no one closer)
Siblings and their descendants (nieces, nephews), by representation
Grandparents, aunts, uncles, first cousins (no one closer)
Half to each side of the family (all to one side if the other has no one)
First cousins once removed (no one closer)
Half to each side, per capita

example.title: Worked example: intestate shares
steps: A New Yorker dies intestate with a $450,000 net estate, a spouse, and two children.
Step 1: The spouse takes $50,000, leaving $400,000.
Step 2: The spouse takes half of that: $200,000.
Step 3: The children split $200,000: $100,000 each.
Answer: spouse $250,000, each child $100,000. With no children, the spouse takes all $450,000.

sections.heading: Voluntary and involuntary alienation
sections.intro: **Voluntary alienation** is a transfer the owner chooses; **involuntary alienation** happens by operation of law.
points: **Eminent domain** is the power to take private property for public use; **condemnation** is the process.
Just compensation, usually market value, is required, so eminent domain is involuntary but paid (U.S. Const. 5th Amend.; NY Const. art. I §7; Eminent Domain Procedure Law).
A partial taking pays for the part taken plus **severance damages** to the remainder.
**Inverse condemnation** is the owner's suit when government effectively takes property without condemning it, such as by repeated sewer flooding.
**PETE:** police power (zoning regulates use without compensation or title transfer), eminent domain, taxation, escheat.
**Accession:** **accretion** adds soil gradually, and the added soil is alluvion. Reliction exposes land as water recedes.
**Avulsion** is a sudden loss to a flood or river change. It generally leaves the legal boundary, and the owner's title, where they were.
**Quiet title** settles competing ownership claims; **partition** divides co-owned land or forces a sale.

head: Transfer
Type
How
rows: Gift of land to the public, such as subdivision streets; by deed, it's dedication by deed
Government conveys land by a land patent
Court divides co-owned land or orders a sale
Accretion or reliction adds land; gradual erosion removes it (a sudden avulsion doesn't move the boundary)
